title: What Higher Ed Should Reclaim from the Right
author: Alejandro J. Ramos
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/joshua-hoehne-
iggWDxHTAUQ-unsplash-680x453.jpg)

Image by Joshua Hoehne.

I woke up this Fourth of July outside the United States, and America followed
me everywhere.

People wished me a happy Fourth. Some did it casually. Others did it with real
excitement, as if they were taking part in the celebration themselves. Back in
the United States, people from all over the world have gathered for the World
Cup—fans from different countries, cultures and political traditions filling
stadiums, streets and cities, eager to experience American food, music, sports
and spectacle.

There has been something moving about it. The United States remains a country
that means something to people who have no obligation to love it. That
deserves a moment of gratitude.

Many of our colleges and universities seem unable to offer one.

On the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, I saw
universities, schools of public policy, democracy centers and civic
institutions use the occasion to warn of decline, democratic fragility and
national failure. Some of those concerns are real. American democracy faces
serious challenges. Our history includes brutality alongside beauty, exclusion
alongside liberty, contradiction alongside aspiration. Any university worthy
of the name should teach that history honestly.

But honesty and contempt are different things. Complexity and cynicism are
different things. Civic education cannot survive if students absorb the idea
that love of country is merely a symptom of ignorance.

This matters because higher education is under serious political pressure. The
Trump administration’s posture toward universities has been aggressive,
punitive and, at times, dangerous. Federal power should not be used to
threaten institutional independence, dictate ideological conformity or punish
universities for dissent. A free society needs colleges and universities that
can teach, research, argue and disagree without fearing political retaliation.

But defending higher education from government overreach does not require
pretending higher education has done nothing to invite public distrust.

I run a nonpartisan nonprofit research institute. I believe deeply in the
value of higher education. I am also a graduate of a school of public policy
whose own master’s thesis focused on administrative bloat, institutional drift
and the misallocation of resources in American higher education. There is much
in our universities that needs reform.

Too many institutions have become fluent in the language of mission while
drifting away from it. They add offices, titles, initiatives, committees and
layers of administration without always asking whether these additions serve
students, faculty or the public. They speak constantly about democracy, yet
often communicate in a language only other academics understand. They claim to
serve communities, while too often remaining distant from the people they
describe.

Then, when political leaders attack them, many Americans shrug. That is the
danger.

Higher education’s defenders often assume the public has been manipulated into
skepticism. Some of that is true. But it is also true that universities have
lost the benefit of the doubt with many families, taxpayers and students. They
see tuition rise. They see bureaucracies grow. They see public statements that
sound more like ideological performance than civic leadership. They see
institutions that lecture the country about democracy while struggling to
model humility, openness and intellectual diversity themselves.

The answer is not to retreat further into the ivory tower. It is to leave it.

Universities should be among the few places in American life capable of
holding two truths at once: America has failed many of its promises, and those
promises remain worth fighting for. The Declaration did not make America
perfect. It gave future generations a standard by which to judge the country’s
imperfections. That is why abolitionists, suffragists, civil-rights leaders,
immigrants, dissidents, veterans, teachers and students have returned again
and again to the language of liberty and equality.

They did not reform America by rejecting the American idea. They reformed
America by demanding that the country live up to it.

That is the lesson higher education should teach on Independence Day.

Patriotism is not blind loyalty. It does not require silence in the face of
injustice. It does not require agreement with the president, Congress, the
Supreme Court, a governor, a mayor or any political party. The American
tradition at its best invites disagreement. It protects dissent. It assumes
citizens can love their country enough to argue about what it should become.

But there is also a difference between dissent and disdain. If every national
celebration becomes another opportunity for institutional scolding, colleges
should not be surprised when much of the country stops listening.

I am the son of immigrants. Both of my parents left Cuba under dictatorship,
one for political reasons and one because authoritarian rule had made economic
life unbearable. They came to the United States because, for all its flaws,
this country represented possibility: freedom, work, speech and a future their
children could inherit and improve.

That story is not unique. It is one version of a story millions of American
families know. People still risk their lives to reach this country. They do so
not because America has always lived up to its creed, but because the creed
still matters.

Higher education should understand that better than anyone.

If colleges and universities want to regain public trust, they should start by
speaking to the public with humility. Teach America’s failures, but do not
reduce America to failure. Celebrate freedom, but do not flatten history into
propaganda. Invite students into citizenship, rather than training them only
in critique. Show that reform can be an act of loyalty to democratic life.

When the federal government oversteps, universities should defend their
independence with moral clarity. That defense will carry further if it is
matched by institutional self-examination.

America does not need universities to pretend everything is fine. It also does
not need them to perform despair. It needs institutions capable of forming
citizens who can tell the truth, love their country and improve it.

That may be the work higher education was always meant to do.
